entities.name: Lucius Quinctius Flamininus
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Lucius Quinctius Flamininus (died 169 BCE) was a Roman politician and general from the distinguished Quinctia gens, whose career spanned the early 2nd century BCE, a period of intense Roman expansion and evolving senatorial ethics. He is primarily significant not only for his military commands and consulship in 192 BCE but also as a prominent example of the moral scrutiny and political puritanism championed by figures like Cato the Elder, which ultimately led to his expulsion from the Senate. His public career illuminates the tensions between traditional aristocratic privilege and emerging standards of public conduct in the Roman Republic.

Flamininus served as consul in 192 BCE alongside Gnaeus Domitius Ahenobarbus, a year marked by preparations for the Roman-Syrian War against Antiochus III. Earlier, as a legate under his more famous brother, Titus Quinctius Flamininus, during the Second Macedonian War (200-197 BCE), Lucius commanded the Roman fleet, playing a crucial role in naval operations against Philip V of Macedon and securing control of the Aegean. This included the capture of Eretria and Carystus in Euboea and successful campaigns against the Spartan tyrant Nabis. His proconsular command in Greece further solidified Roman influence in the region, particularly after the decisive Battle of Cynoscephalae.

Flamininus's most enduring legacy, however, stems from his public humiliation and expulsion from the Senate by the censor Cato the Elder in 184 BCE. Cato cited various charges of moral turpitude and excessive behavior, including an infamous incident where Flamininus, during his consulship, allegedly ordered the execution of a condemned Gallic prisoner to entertain a male lover. This act, whether fully true or exaggerated by Cato, served as a potent symbol of the moral decline Cato perceived within the Roman aristocracy and marked a pivotal moment in the censorial assertion of moral authority over the senatorial class.
